Mars Survival Atlas is an interactive 3D platform developed by Team ATHAR | آثار for NASA Space Apps Challenge 2026, addressing the “Interplanetary Survival Guide: Martian Map” challenge.

Our platform transforms complex Martian geographic and environmental data into an accessible exploration and mission-planning experience. Using NASA Mars Trek imagery and MOLA-derived elevation data, users can explore Mars, visualize terrain slopes, select locations, and compare direct routes with alternative paths that account for terrain steepness.

The platform also incorporates selected historical NASA MEDA data, a separately identified Mars Climate Database result, mission landmarks, and an illustrative day-and-night lighting feature. Environmental data integration remains under development.

By combining scientific datasets with interactive visualization and experimental route planning, Mars Survival Atlas helps users understand the geographical and environmental challenges of exploring Mars. Our goal is to make planetary data easier to interpret and demonstrate how terrain analysis can support future mission-planning research.

The platform is an educational prototype, not a validated rover navigation system.
details:
Mars Survival Atlas — Project Details

Project Overview

Mars Survival Atlas is an interactive, browser-based 3D platform developed by Team ATHAR | آثار for NASA Space Apps Challenge 2026.

Our project addresses the “Interplanetary Survival Guide: Martian Map” challenge by combining Martian terrain visualization, geographic analysis, experimental route planning, and environmental information into one accessible digital experience.

Instead of presenting planetary datasets as separate technical resources, we bring them together in an interactive environment that allows users to explore Mars and investigate challenges associated with surface exploration.

How Does It Work?

Interactive 3D Mars Exploration

Users can rotate, zoom into, and explore a three-dimensional representation of Mars. The globe incorporates NASA Mars Trek imagery and allows users to investigate selected geographic landmarks and surface regions.

Terrain and Slope Analysis

The platform uses elevation information derived from NASA's Mars Orbiter Laser Altimeter (MOLA) to visualize terrain characteristics and surface slopes. These layers help users understand how elevation changes and steep terrain can affect surface travel.

Experimental Route Planning

Users can select locations and compare a direct route with an alternative calculated using a slope-weighted A* pathfinding approach.

The algorithm considers both travel distance and sampled terrain steepness, illustrating how a slightly longer route may avoid steeper terrain.

In one demonstrated comparison:

  • Direct route: 809.8 km, maximum sampled slope 5.7°, average sampled slope 1.0°.
  • Lower-slope route: 837.0 km, maximum sampled slope 4.6°, average sampled slope 0.6°.

This demonstrates a trade-off between route length and terrain conditions. The results are experimental and do not represent validated rover navigation or a guarantee of safety.

Environmental Context

The platform includes selected historical measurements from NASA's Mars Environmental Dynamics Analyzer (MEDA), a precomputed climatology result from the Mars Climate Database, and an illustrative day-and-night lighting feature.

These features help users understand that surface exploration involves environmental conditions as well as geography. Some environmental data integration remains under development.

Technologies and Development Tools

We developed Mars Survival Atlas as a web-based software prototype using:

  • React and JavaScript for the interactive interface and application functionality.
  • Three.js for rendering and controlling the 3D Mars globe.
  • Vite for the web development and build process.
  • NASA Mars Trek for planetary imagery and geographic context.
  • NASA MOLA-derived data for elevation and slope visualization.
  • NASA MEDA data for selected historical environmental measurements.
  • Mars Climate Database for a separately identified climatological data result.
  • A* pathfinding for experimental terrain-aware route comparison.
  • Netlify for hosting the publicly accessible web application.

The current prototype is software-based and does not require specialized physical hardware or a robotic rover.

Creativity and Innovation

The creativity of Mars Survival Atlas lies in combining scientific planetary datasets with interactive exploration and route comparison.

Rather than displaying a static map, our platform allows users to investigate terrain, examine slope information, and observe how different route-planning priorities can produce different paths.

The project also brings geographical and environmental information into a single experience, making complex concepts more accessible to students, researchers, and space enthusiasts.

Our approach emphasizes the relationship between scientific data, visualization, and decision-making.

Benefits and Intended Impact

Mars Survival Atlas aims to:

  • Make Martian geographic and environmental data easier to explore and understand.
  • Demonstrate why terrain steepness matters when considering surface routes.
  • Support education in planetary science, programming, geographic analysis, and space exploration.
  • Encourage students to use publicly available NASA datasets to develop practical technological concepts.
  • Provide a foundation for future research into more advanced terrain-aware mission-planning tools.

Our long-term vision is to expand the platform into a more comprehensive environment for exploring Martian surface conditions and evaluating hypothetical mission scenarios.

Design Considerations and Limitations

During development, our team considered scientific grounding, accessibility, terrain trade-offs, clarity, and technical limitations.

We prioritized recognizable planetary data sources and distinguished NASA datasets from external scientific resources. We designed the platform to run in a web browser and considered both distance and slope when developing the experimental route-planning feature.

The current route-planning model does not account for every factor required for real Mars missions, such as detailed obstacle detection, rover-specific mobility constraints, energy consumption, or operational safety verification.

The lighting simulation is illustrative, and environmental data integration is not yet fully complete.

Mars Survival Atlas is therefore an educational and exploratory prototype rather than a mission-certified navigation system.

Future Development

Our next development goals include improving environmental data integration, refining terrain analysis, incorporating additional mission-planning constraints, and evaluating route-planning approaches against more detailed planetary datasets.

We also aim to improve the platform's usability and expand the number of regions and scientific datasets available for exploration.

Ultimately, Mars Survival Atlas demonstrates how accessible software, scientific data, and creative problem-solving can contribute to a deeper understanding of the challenges of exploring another planet.
